title: The AO3 Shutdown Is Pitting Fanfic Readers Against Authors
gist: Archive of Our Own (AO3), hosting 18.8M+ fan works, went dark on October 29 after a security incident and may stay offline up to four weeks; readers re-uploaded saved stories to mirror sites and Google Drive libraries without author consent, inflaming author fears about AI scraping and loss of control. Anti-AI writing platform Ellipsus is a beneficiary, reporting sign-ups up more than 500% since the outage.

insights.claim: Archive of Our Own (AO3), which hosts more than 18.8 million fan works across hundreds of thousands of fandoms and is among the most visited websites in the world, went offline on October 29 due to a security incident and announced it would remain down for up to four weeks.
insights.speaker: Michaela Makusha
insights.so_what: A single nonprofit archive is a single point of failure for a huge creator community; a security incident there creates instant demand for alternative hosting.
insights.locator: Hosting more than 18.8 million fan works

insights.claim: Within days of the AO3 outage, readers uploaded locally saved fan fiction to shared Google Drive libraries and mirror sites such as Squidgeworld and AO3.Life without authors' permission, breaking fanfic norms of asking consent.
insights.speaker: Michaela Makusha
insights.so_what: Platform outages trigger uncontrolled redistribution of user-generated content, raising rights, security and scraping exposure for creators and hosts.
insights.locator: Within days, readers who had saved stories

insights.claim: The Archive Salvation Google Drive project, a collective archive of fan fiction downloaded from AO3, was hacked and made inaccessible, per a November 3 moderator statement, though the group continues sharing fanfics via a closed Discord server.
insights.speaker: Michaela Makusha
insights.so_what: Ad hoc community mirrors are themselves fragile and attack targets, pushing activity into closed channels like Discord.
insights.quote: our drive was controversial and very public, so the hacker is most likely someone who stands against drives like this in general.

themes.theme: Author control, security and AI-scraping fears

insights.claim: Fan fiction authors view unauthorized mass re-uploads of their work to giant drive libraries as both a security risk (potential malware vectors) and an amplifier of fears that their work will be scraped for AI training.
insights.speaker: Michaela Makusha
insights.so_what: Creator anxiety about AI scraping is a live demand driver for hosting platforms that offer access control and anti-AI positioning.
insights.quote: One bad actor could put malware in that drive.
insights.locator: “To me it’s a security risk,” Avery

insights.claim: The AO3 outage exposed that fan fiction authors have little practical protection once their work is posted online, as copies persist on mirrors and drives they cannot fully track or remove.
insights.speaker: Michaela Makusha
insights.so_what: Content permanence and weak takedown tools are structural weaknesses of open UGC archives; tools offering author control address a real gap.
insights.quote: the internet is forever for better or for worse

insights.claim: Fandom's distrust of mass redistribution has historical roots: cease-and-desist notices and takedown controversies on Fanfiction.net and LiveJournal in the 1990s and 2000s led to AO3's founding.
insights.speaker: Michaela Makusha
insights.so_what: Community memory of takedowns shapes platform loyalty; any host that appears to expose works to removal or scraping risks backlash.

insights.claim: Ellipsus, an anti-AI collaborative writing platform founded in 2022, says new sign-ups are up more than 500% since the AO3 outage began, with views of its public reader links also increasing heavily.
insights.speaker: Michaela Makusha
insights.so_what: Outages at dominant community platforms can rapidly shift users to smaller alternatives that differentiate on control and anti-AI stance.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Ellipsus, a collaborative writing platform

insights.claim: Ellipsus differentiates on author control—letting writers choose who sees their work and how readers interact—and had already tailored features for fan fiction writers before the AO3 outage, including a button that exports work directly to AO3.
insights.speaker: Michaela Makusha
insights.so_what: Granular access control is the product wedge for creator platforms competing against open archives in an era of AI scraping fears.
insights.quote: We know that people want a space to not only write but share new writing, in a way that feels safe for them,

insights.claim: Fan fiction has broken into the mainstream, driven by shows like Heated Rivalry, adaptations of former fan fiction such as SenLinYu's Alchemised (originally published on AO3) into novels, and viral short-form sharing on social media.
insights.speaker: Michaela Makusha
insights.so_what: Fan fiction is becoming an IP pipeline for publishing and TV, raising the commercial stakes around who controls and distributes these works.
insights.locator: Another reason the outage has felt so fraught

insights.claim: Much of the backlash over the AO3 outage stems from a mismatch between how large the fan fiction community actually is—including casual fans outside core fandom—and how small and norm-bound it still feels to many participants.
insights.speaker: Michaela Makusha
insights.so_what: Community norms built for small groups break at mainstream scale, a recurring source of conflict for UGC platforms.
insights.locator: Rosenberg, who is writing a book on fandom
